name: Standing desk height
seoDesc: Standing desk height: work out your weight from the calories burned standing. A free everyday life calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Standing desk height calculator is a free, no-sign-up everyday life tool. Fill in the 5 fields it asks for and it works out your weight straight away, with the formula shown underneath. Think of it as a shortcut for a practical question that turns up in daily life. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Standing desk height calculator work?
sections.html:
The Standing desk height calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports your weight in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (your height (while wearing shoes) and your height (in shoes)); then you type in how many hours spent standing? and the calories burned standing.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 56 options, such as 150 cm, 151 cm and 152 cm. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 45 options, such as 4' 11", 4' 11 ½" and 5'. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in hours. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in kilocalories. The unit chip switches it to any of the 33 supported units.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.

2 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Standing desk height calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Your weight=(10 ÷ 21) × calories burned standing ÷ how many hours spent standing?
Your weight=(40 ÷ 21) × which is ÷ how many hours spent standing?
Unit factor=(((Determining variable > 0) ? ( 1 ) : ( 127 ÷ 50 )))
Height=(((Determining variable > 0) ? ( height in ) : ( height cm )))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Take Your height (while wearing shoes) set to 170 cm, Your height (in shoes) set to 5' 7", How many hours spent standing? = 10 hrs and Calories burned standing = 10 kcal. The calculator returns Your weight = 0.5534 kg and Which is = 2.5 kcal.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Your weight = 0.5534 kg and Which is = 2.5 kcal should be roughly the size you expected from Your height (while wearing shoes) set to 170 cm and Your height (in shoes) set to 5' 7".

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Time, opening in hours
  • Energy, opening in kilocalories
  • Energy, opening in kilocalories

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Standing desk height calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 1 figures keep coming back — the calories burned standing — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the Standing desk height calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns your weight, derived from the calories burned standing. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Standing desk height calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the calories burned standing, which is 5 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter your weight in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Your weight opens in kilograms and the chip beside it offers 29 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Your weight = 0.5534 kg. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Standing desk height calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
